justification: The only primary human genetic evidence is Muona et al. (PMID 25401298), which identified a recurrent de novo c.959G>A (p.Arg320His) KCNC1 variant in 11 unrelated exome-sequenced individuals plus 2 in a secondary cohort with progressive myoclonus epilepsy, supported by functional demonstration of a dominant-negative loss of function. PMID 27629860 is a review of MEAK that restates this finding as background rather than reporting new probands, so it counts as citation, not independent replication. Because only one primary study with original patient variant data can be cited, the evidence is capped at "Existing" by the stated rule, although the number of independent de novo probands within that one study makes a de facto established relationship plausible. Remaining literature (Kv3.1 knockout mice without seizures, 4-AP/levetiracetam pharmacology, auditory brainstem expression, opioid dependence GWAS) is supportive biology or irrelevant, supporting only a small "Hypothesized" weight.

justification: The only human, autism-specific genetic evidence is a single case report of an interstitial 4q31.3–q33 deletion in a child with autism, rendering him hemizygous for GRIA2 along with GLRA3, GLRB, NPY1R and NPY5R (PMID 15090072); because this is a multigene CNV in one proband, it cannot single out GRIA2 and cannot support "Established". Supporting but non-autism human data include GRIA2-containing copy-number changes in intellectual disability cohorts (PMID 19623214, 20358617, 22669415), and GRIA2 variation linked to lithium response/schizophrenia (PMID 19448189, 23378337, 25842862), which are different phenotypes. The remaining literature is animal/in vitro (Shank3, neuroligin-1, RAB39B, GluD1, Mthfr, PMCA2 models) showing GluA2 dysregulation in ASD-relevant mechanisms, which is classic "Hypothesized" support rather than human genetic evidence. Thus the balance favors limited, non-definitive human association (Existing), with substantial residual probability that the evidence is purely biological/animal-based (Hypothesized).

justification: No article in this set reports LRRTM2 variants identified in autism probands or families; the ASD mentions are background statements accompanying neurexin/neuroligin biology (PMIDs 21155806, 20519524, 24587117, 24005312). The only human genetic study (PMID 23326251) concerns a multigene 5q31 microdeletion with intellectual disability/DD—not ASD—and its targeted sequencing of LRRTM2 in 330 ID/DD patients was negative, so it cannot establish a gene-specific association. PMID 21424692 reports truncating NRXN2/NRXN1 mutations in ASD patients and uses LRRTM2 only as an in vitro binding partner assay, which supports pathway relevance rather than LRRTM2 variant evidence. The strongest support is therefore biological: LRRTM2 is a postsynaptic neurexin ligand driving excitatory synapse development, a pathway implicated in ASD—fitting "Hypothesized." A small residual probability is left for "Existing" in case the 5q31/synaptic-pathway data are credited as limited human evidence.

justification: Essentially all human genetic evidence for CHRNA1 in this corpus concerns congenital myasthenic syndromes, fetal akinesia/multiple pterygium syndrome, and autoimmune myasthenia gravis (PMIDs 20157724, 20562457, 18806275, 23037934, 17687331) — neuromuscular junction phenotypes with no relation to epilepsy. The only epilepsy co-mention is a porcine study of congenital progressive ataxia/spastic paresis in which CHRNA1 was listed as a positional/physiological candidate because the syntenic human region harbors channel genes linked to epilepsy; that study was in pigs, found no CHRNA1 variants, and explicitly rejected the hypothesis (PMID 17868079). No human study here reports CHRNA1 variants in epilepsy patients, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported. A small amount of weight goes to Hypothesized only because a neuronal-type ligand-gated cholinergic receptor subunit family has loose biological plausibility and was once nominated as a candidate, though CHRNA1 itself is the muscle subunit.

justification: None of the provided articles report any genetic variant in TRAPPC4 associated with epilepsy or seizures in humans. The Parkinson's disease study (PMID 20035503) found TRAPPC4 differentially expressed in substantia nigra neurons but the validated risk variant was in PDXK, not TRAPPC4, and the phenotype is not epilepsy. The eQTL/epistasis study (PMID 27052692) concerns smallpox vaccine response and apoptosis genes, entirely unrelated to epilepsy. The mouse microwave-exposure study (PMID 26383594) mentions synbindin (sbdn, the TRAPPC4 product) in a protein interaction network related to learning and memory and long-term potentiation — a non-human, indirect neurological link that provides only the faintest biological rationale, not an epilepsy connection. Therefore the relationship is best described as novel, with a small allowance for a hypothesized neuronal/synaptic role.

justification: Every article provided concerns MYH2 (myosin heavy chain IIa) in the context of skeletal muscle disease — recessive and dominant myosin myopathies with ophthalmoplegia, inclusion body myopathy 3, distal arthrogryposis, and related myosinopathies — or incidental muscle gene-expression studies (masseter muscle, cremaster muscle). None of the papers examine autism spectrum disorder, neurodevelopmental phenotypes, behavior, or brain expression, and no genetic association, functional, or animal-model evidence links MYH2 to ASD. The co-mentions are nonexistent rather than merely incidental; there is no logical biological bridge presented between fast type 2A muscle fiber myosin and ASD. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel.
